title: SMTP Service Extension for Message Size Declaration
summary: Defines an SMTP extension that lets a client declare the size of a message in advance so the server can decline it, perhaps temporarily, before the whole thing is sent. It is an Internet Standard.

eli5.summary: Tell the post office how big the package is before dropping it off, so they can refuse it without you carrying it in.

questions: what is the smtp size extension
how does smtp reject large messages early
how does smtp ehlo size work
subtitle: Lets an email client announce a message's size up front so the server can refuse it before it is sent.

tldr.problem: With plain SMTP, a client only learns that a message is too large or that the server lacks space after it has sent the whole message, which the server then discards.
tldr.mechanism: The server advertises a SIZE keyword in its EHLO reply, optionally with its maximum size. The client can add a SIZE parameter to MAIL FROM, and the server answers with 452 or 552 if it cannot take a message of that size.
tldr.outcome: Large messages can be declined, temporarily or permanently, before any data moves. The RFC is an Internet Standard and obsoletes RFC 1653.

today: RFC 1870 is an Internet Standard (STD 10) and is not marked as obsoleted or updated. It obsoletes RFC 1653.

sections.title: Why Declare a Message Size
sections.content:
MIME allows many kinds of data to travel in Internet mail, so SMTP is expected to carry a much wider range of message sizes. That affects the resources, such as disk space, that a receiving server needs.

With unextended SMTP, a client can only be told about a size failure after it has sent the entire message, which the server then throws away. If both sides support this extension, the failure can be detected before any transfer starts.
sections.eli5: Without this, you carry the whole heavy box to the counter and only then hear that it is too big. With it, you ask first.

sections.title: The Size Declaration Extension
sections.content:
The extension is named Message Size Declaration and is announced with the EHLO keyword SIZE. It adds no new SMTP verbs. It does three things:

  • The SIZE keyword in the EHLO reply may carry one optional decimal parameter: the fixed maximum message size, in bytes, that the server will accept. A value of 0 means no fixed maximum is in force. If the parameter is omitted, nothing is said about a maximum.
  • The MAIL FROM command gains an optional SIZE parameter whose value is a decimal number, 1 to 20 digits, giving the size of the message to be sent.
  • The maximum length of a MAIL FROM line grows by 26 characters to make room for it.

A client discovers support by sending EHLO. If the server answers with code 250 and the reply includes SIZE, the extension is available.
sections.eli5: The server puts a sign on the door saying how big a package it takes, and the sender can write the package size on the form before handing it over.

sections.title: How Size Is Counted
sections.content:
The message size is the number of octets, counting CR-LF pairs, that the client sends after it receives reply code 354 to DATA. The terminating dot and doubled quoting dots are not counted. The declared message size is the client's estimate for a particular message, and the fixed maximum message size is the largest message the server will ever accept.

The declared size should include the header, the body and the CR-LF sequences between lines. Ideally it equals the true size, but an exact count may be infeasible, so a client may use a heuristic estimate. The RFC says such heuristics should be chosen so that the declared size is usually larger than the real one. Only one SIZE parameter may appear in a single MAIL command, and servers MUST NOT use it to find the end of content in DATA.
sections.eli5: You measure the package as best you can, and it is better to guess a little too big than too small.

sections.title: Server and Client Behavior
sections.content:
On a MAIL command with SIZE, the server checks the declared size against its fixed maximum. If the declared size is smaller, it may also check whether it has enough resources to buffer the message and keep it in stable storage until delivery. Besides the usual MAIL errors, it can answer:

  • 452 insufficient system storage when it lacks space now but may have it later.
  • 552 message size exceeds fixed maximum message size when the size is larger than its fixed maximum.

On a 452, the client should send RSET or QUIT and retry later. On a 552, it should send RSET or QUIT straight away and treat the message as undeliverable, notifying the sender if a sender address was present.

A 250 reply is not an absolute guarantee. Clients must still handle 452 and 552 after DATA or after the transfer. A server should not return 552 after the transfer unless the actual size exceeds the declared size, though it may accept a message that is somewhat larger. A client may declare a size smaller than the real one, but then a 250 gives no assurance.

A server may also return 452 or 552 in reply to a RCPT command for a specific recipient. After a 452 the client may requeue for that recipient. After a 552 it may not.
sections.eli5: The clerk can say "come back later, we are full" or "we never take packages that big". Hearing yes still does not promise the package will be taken if you fibbed about its size.

sections.title: Minimal Usage and an Example
sections.content:
A minimal client may only compare its message size with the number in the EHLO SIZE parameter, without ever sending the extended MAIL command. It then cannot learn about temporary limits or per-recipient limits. A minimal server may just advertise its limit, or advertise that there is none, but it must accept the extended MAIL command and return 552 when the declared size exceeds its fixed limit.

If a server sends SIZE with no parameter, it should not give a positive 250 to a MAIL with a size without first checking that it has the resources, and if possible it should reserve the space.

The RFC's example shows a server advertising SIZE 1000000, a client declaring SIZE=500000, and then one recipient accepted, one refused with 552 and one deferred with 452.
sections.eli5: Even a simple sender can just read the sign on the door. A fancier one also fills in the size on the form to get more precise answers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC notes that the size information and the extended MAIL command can conceivably make a crude denial of service attack somewhat quicker and easier to devise. It adds that, unless implementations are very weak, the extension does not create any vulnerability that SMTP did not already have. It addresses no issues about trusted systems or release of information.
sections.eli5: Telling people your size limits might help a troublemaker a tiny bit, but not more than they could already do.
